q: Name the pinned vessel.
options: Blood capillary
Lacteal
Hepatic portal vein
Central vein

why.correct: The lacteal is the lymphatic capillary in the center of each villus. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, but they pass through the gaps between the lacteal's cells.
options: The blood capillary is the red loop around the lacteal. Sugars and amino acids enter it; chylomicrons are too large.
Correct. Chylomicrons enter the lacteal and travel in lymph.
The hepatic portal vein collects blood from the villus capillaries far downstream; it is not in the villus.
Central veins are in the liver lobules, not in the villi.

q: Name the pinned enzyme.
options: Sucrase
Maltase
Lactase
α-Dextrinase

why.correct: Lactase, a brush border enzyme, splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
options: Sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose.
Maltase splits maltose into two glucose.
Correct. Lactase splits lactose.
α-Dextrinase cuts the branch bonds of α-dextrins.

q: Put the steps of starch digestion and absorption in order.
options: Salivary amylase starts cutting starch in the mouth
Pancreatic amylase cuts starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins in the small intestine
Brush border maltase and α-dextrinase split these into glucose
Glucose enters the absorptive cell with sodium through SGLT1
Glucose leaves the cell by facilitated diffusion across the basolateral membrane
Glucose travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver

why.correct: Amylase in saliva, then from the pancreas, cuts starch into short pieces. Brush border enzymes finish them into glucose at the membrane. SGLT1 brings glucose in with sodium, a basolateral carrier lets it out, and the villus capillaries drain into the hepatic portal vein.

q: Put the steps of protein digestion and absorption in order.
options: Pepsin cuts proteins into large polypeptides in the stomach
Trypsin and chymotrypsin cut the polypeptides into shorter peptides in the duodenum
Carboxypeptidase and brush border aminopeptidase remove amino acids from the chain ends
Amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides enter the absorptive cells on carriers
Peptidases inside the cell split dipeptides and tripeptides into amino acids
Amino acids leave the cell and enter the villus capillaries

why.correct: Pepsin starts, cutting inside chains. The pancreatic enzymes trypsin and chymotrypsin cut further inside the chains, and carboxypeptidase and aminopeptidase trim from the ends. Amino acids and small peptides enter the cells; the peptides are split inside, and amino acids leave into the blood.

q: Put the steps of fat digestion and absorption in order.
options: Bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets
Pancreatic lipase splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides
Micelles carry fatty acids and monoglycerides to the brush border
Fatty acids and monoglycerides enter the absorptive cell and are rebuilt into triglycerides
Triglycerides are packaged into chylomicrons and leave the cell by exocytosis
Chylomicrons enter a lacteal and travel in lymph to the thoracic duct

why.correct: Emulsification gives lipase more surface; lipase makes fatty acids and monoglycerides; micelles ferry them through the water next to the brush border; inside the cell they are rebuilt and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteal instead.

q: An adult with low lactase drinks two large glasses of milk on an empty stomach. Predict the change in each variable over the next few hours, compared with a person with high lactase drinking the same milk.

variables.name: Lactose reaching the colon
variables.why: Too little lactase is left at the brush border to split the lactose, so much of it passes through the small intestine intact.

variables.name: Water in the lumen of the small intestine
variables.why: Unabsorbed lactose is a solute that stays in the lumen and holds water there by osmosis.

variables.name: Hydrogen in the exhaled breath
variables.why: Colon bacteria ferment the lactose and make hydrogen; some is absorbed into the blood and breathed out.

variables.name: Water content of the stool
variables.why: The extra water, plus the solutes fermentation adds, is more than the colon can absorb, so the stool becomes loose.

variables.name: Rise in blood glucose after drinking
variables.why: Undigested lactose yields no glucose or galactose for SGLT1 to absorb, so blood glucose rises less than it would after the milk in a person with high lactase.

why.correct: Without enough lactase, lactose cannot be split or absorbed. It holds water in the small intestine by osmosis and is fermented by colon bacteria into gas and acids, giving bloating, hydrogen on the breath and osmotic diarrhea, while little of its sugar reaches the blood.

q: A patient takes a weight-loss drug that blocks pancreatic lipase in the gut. Predict the change in each variable after a fatty meal, compared with the same meal without the drug.

variables.name: Monoglycerides formed in the lumen
variables.why: Lipase is the enzyme that splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides; blocking it leaves the triglycerides intact.

variables.name: Chylomicrons entering the lacteals
variables.why: Intact triglycerides cannot enter micelles or cross the brush border, so absorptive cells have less fat to package.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Undigested triglyceride passes through the gut and leaves in the stool.

variables.name: Absorption of vitamin D from the meal
variables.why: Vitamins that dissolve in fat are absorbed with micelles and leave in chylomicrons, so less fat absorption means less of them absorbed.

variables.name: Glucose absorption from the meal's starch
variables.why: Starch is digested by amylase and brush border enzymes and absorbed through SGLT1, none of which need lipase.

why.correct: Blocking lipase stops the splitting step, so triglycerides are neither taken into micelles nor absorbed. Fat and the vitamins that travel with it are lost in the feces, while carbohydrate digestion and absorption carry on unchanged.

q: In an experiment on intestinal tissue, a drug blocks the sodium–potassium pumps on the basolateral membrane of the absorptive cells. SGLT1 itself is untouched. What happens to glucose absorption?
options: It stops once sodium inside the cell rises and the gradient collapses
It continues unchanged
It speeds up
It continues at the same rate by facilitated diffusion

why.correct: SGLT1 uses the energy of sodium moving down its gradient into the cell. The pumps keep sodium inside the cell low. Once they stop, sodium inside rises, the gradient collapses, and SGLT1 can no longer pull glucose in against its own gradient.
options: Correct. With the pumps stopped, sodium leaks in and is not removed, the gradient collapses, and SGLT1 loses its energy source.
SGLT1 uses no ATP directly, but it depends on the sodium gradient that the ATP-using pumps maintain.
Sodium building up inside the cell shrinks the gradient, which slows SGLT1 rather than speeding it.
Facilitated diffusion moves glucose only down its own gradient, so it cannot keep absorption going at the same rate once lumen glucose falls.

q: A child with cholera is losing liters of watery stool. The toxin makes the intestinal lining secrete chloride, and sodium and water follow. Nurses give a drink of water, salt and glucose. Why does the glucose help?
options: Glucose kills the cholera bacteria in the lumen
Glucose blocks the chloride secretion caused by the toxin
Glucose pulls sodium in through SGLT1, and water follows
Glucose is the main fuel the child's colon needs to absorb water

why.correct: The toxin drives secretion but leaves SGLT1 working. Each glucose that enters through SGLT1 brings two sodium ions with it. The absorbed sodium and glucose raise the solute on the blood side, and water follows by osmosis, rehydrating the child even while secretion goes on.
options: Glucose does not kill bacteria; it feeds most of them.
The chloride secretion continues. The solution works by adding absorption, not by blocking secretion.
Correct. Sodium-glucose cotransport is the basis of oral rehydration.
The colon's epithelial cells burn mainly butyrate from bacteria, and fuel is not what limits absorption here.

q: Using the figure, what share of the fluid that reaches the colon does the colon absorb?
options: About 14%
About 89%
About 50%
Nearly 98%

why.correct: 1,400 mL reaches the colon (1,200 from the small intestine plus 200 of its own mucous secretions). It absorbs 1,250 mL. 1,250 ÷ 1,400 = 0.89, about 89%, leaving 150 mL in the feces.
options: 14% is the share of the whole day's fluid that the colon absorbs (1,250 of about 9,200 mL), not the share of what reaches it.
Correct. The colon absorbs most of what it receives.
Half would leave about 700 mL in the feces; the figure shows 150 mL.
About 98% is the share absorbed by the whole gut, small intestine and colon together.

q: Why do absorbed long-chain fats reach the blood through the lymph instead of entering the villus capillaries directly?
options: Bile salts carry the fats straight into the lacteals
Lymph moves faster than blood through the villus
The villus capillaries are continuous, with an unbroken wall
Chylomicrons are too large for the blood capillaries

why.correct: Absorbed long-chain fats leave the cell packaged as chylomicrons, large particles that cannot cross the wall of the villus blood capillaries. The lacteal's cells have wide gaps between them that let chylomicrons in.
options: Bile salts stay in the lumen and are reabsorbed in the ileum. The fats leave the absorptive cell as chylomicrons, without bile salts.
Lymph flows much more slowly than blood.
The villus capillaries are fenestrated and take up sugars, amino acids and short-chain fatty acids; their pores are simply too small for chylomicrons.
Correct. Size decides the route.

q: A stone completely blocks the common bile duct for several weeks. Select every substance whose absorption falls sharply.
options: Long-chain fatty acids
Vitamin K
Glucose
Cholesterol
Amino acids
Vitamin D

why.correct: Without bile salts, fat is poorly emulsified and no micelles form, so long-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and the vitamins that dissolve in fat, such as D and K, are poorly absorbed. Glucose and amino acids are water-soluble and absorbed by carriers that do not need bile.
options: Correct. Long-chain fatty acids need micelles to reach the brush border.
Correct. Vitamin K travels with fat in micelles; its loss is why obstructive jaundice can cause bleeding.
Glucose is absorbed through SGLT1, which does not need bile.
Correct. Cholesterol is absorbed from micelles.
Amino acids use carriers powered by sodium, not micelles.
Correct. Vitamin D dissolves in fat and is absorbed with it.

q: A 45-year-old man had the last meter of his ileum removed eight years ago. He eats a normal diet and his stomach is healthy. He now has a large-cell anemia and numb feet. What is the most likely cause?
options: Loss of the site where B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed
Loss of intrinsic factor production
Loss of pancreatic proteases that free B12 from haptocorrin
Loss of the lactase needed to absorb B12

why.correct: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed only in the terminal ileum, by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Removing it stops B12 absorption. The liver's store lasts three to five years, so the deficiency appears years after surgery.
options: Correct. The terminal ileum is the only site where B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed.
His stomach is healthy, so parietal cells still make intrinsic factor.
His pancreas is not affected by removing the ileum.
Lactase splits lactose; it has no role in B12 absorption.

q: Complete the route of vitamin B12: acid and pepsin free B12 from food and it binds haptocorrin → ____ → B12 binds intrinsic factor → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
options: Pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin in the duodenum
Bile salts carry B12 into micelles in the jejunum
Lactase splits B12 away from haptocorrin at the brush border
Chylomicrons carry B12 into the lacteals of the villi

why.correct: Haptocorrin holds B12 through the stomach. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases such as trypsin digest haptocorrin, freeing B12 to bind intrinsic factor. That is why pancreatic failure can reduce B12 absorption.
options: Correct. Pancreatic proteases hand B12 over to intrinsic factor.
B12 is water-soluble and is not carried in micelles.
Lactase splits lactose; it does not act on proteins.
B12 is absorbed by endocytosis in the ileum and leaves the cell into the blood, not in chylomicrons.

q: A 25-year-old woman gets bloating, gas and loose stools about two hours after drinking milk, but eats hard cheese without trouble. She has never had hives or wheezing. Which explanation fits best?
options: A milk allergy: IgE against milk proteins
Low lactase: lactose reaches her colon and is fermented
A pancreatic lipase deficiency: she cannot digest milk fat
Too much lactase: glucose floods her colon

why.correct: Milk contains a lot of lactose; hard cheese contains very little. Undigested lactose holds water in the gut and is fermented by colon bacteria, causing gas, bloating and osmotic diarrhea a couple of hours later. This is lactose intolerance, not an immune reaction.
options: A milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk proteins, usually with hives, vomiting or wheezing, and cheese contains the same proteins.
Correct. Her symptoms follow the lactose content of the food.
A lipase deficiency would cause fatty stools after any fatty food, including cheese.
More lactase would digest lactose completely, and glucose is absorbed in the small intestine.

q: A student described what happens to fat after lipase has digested it. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Fatty acids and monoglycerides join bile salts in micelles
At the brush border they leave the micelles and enter the absorptive cell
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum rebuilds them into triglycerides
Triglycerides are packaged with cholesterol and protein into chylomicrons
Chylomicrons enter the villus blood capillaries and go to the liver in the hepatic portal vein

why.correct: Chylomicrons are too large for the villus blood capillaries. They enter the lacteals and travel in lymph through the thoracic duct into the veins where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet, bypassing the liver at first.
options: This step is right. Micelles carry the digested lipids through the water next to the brush border.
This step is right. The lipids cross the apical membrane; the bile salts stay in the lumen.
This step is right. Rebuilding keeps free fatty acids inside the cell low.
This step is right. Chylomicrons are triglyceride and cholesterol wrapped in phospholipid and protein.
This is the error. Chylomicrons enter the lacteals, not the blood capillaries.

q: What are the final products of nucleic acid digestion that the absorptive cells take up?
options: Whole nucleotides, taken up intact by carriers
Amino acids and glucose from the nucleic acid chains
Short RNA chains, taken up by endocytosis
Pentose sugars, nitrogenous bases and phosphate

why.correct: Pancreatic nucleases cut DNA and RNA into nucleotides, and brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases split the nucleotides into their parts: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and phosphate. These are absorbed by active transport.
options: Nucleotides are split further at the brush border before absorption.
Amino acids and glucose come from proteins and carbohydrates, not nucleic acids.
Pancreatic nucleases cut RNA chains down to nucleotides.
Correct. Nucleotides are split into their three parts.

q: A child has an inherited defect in the brush border carrier for a group of neutral amino acids. Yet blood levels of those amino acids after a protein meal are only mildly low. What best explains this?
options: Those amino acids diffuse freely through the lipid bilayer of the brush border
Much of them enters inside dipeptides and tripeptides on another carrier
The colon absorbs all the amino acids the small intestine misses
Pepsin converts them into other amino acids that use working carriers

why.correct: Dipeptides and tripeptides enter on their own carrier, powered by hydrogen ions, and are split inside the cell. Neutral amino acids locked inside those short peptides still get in, so the defective single-amino-acid carrier is partly bypassed.
options: Amino acids are charged or polar and need carriers to cross the membrane.
Correct. Peptide absorption provides a second route in.
Very little amino acid absorption happens in the colon.
Pepsin cuts peptide bonds; it does not turn one amino acid into another.

q: Celiac disease flattens the villi and damages the brush border. After a starchy meal, which products would you expect to build up in the lumen?
options: Whole starch
Glucose
Maltose and α-dextrins
Galactose

why.correct: Pancreatic amylase works in the lumen and still cuts starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins. The last step, by maltase and α-dextrinase, happens on the brush border, which is damaged. So the partly digested pieces build up, unabsorbed.
options: Pancreatic amylase works in the lumen, not on the brush border, so starch is still cut into pieces.
Glucose is released by maltase and α-dextrinase on the brush border, which is damaged, so little is made.
Correct. The brush border step fails, so its substrates accumulate.
Starch is made only of glucose; galactose comes from lactose.

q: Which statement about carboxypeptidase is correct?
options: It comes from the pancreas and removes amino acids from the carboxyl end of a chain
It is fixed to the brush border and removes amino acids from the amino end of a chain
It is made by the stomach's chief cells and works best in acid
It digests carbohydrates that carry carboxyl groups

why.correct: Carboxypeptidase arrives in pancreatic juice as an inactive precursor, is activated by trypsin, and removes amino acids one at a time from the end of a chain that has a free carboxyl group. Its partner at the other end is aminopeptidase, on the brush border.
options: Correct. Pancreatic source, carboxyl end.
That describes aminopeptidase, which works from the amino end.
Pepsin is the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme. Carboxypeptidase works in the near-neutral small intestine.
"Carboxy" refers to the carboxyl end of a protein chain, not to carbohydrate; carboxypeptidase digests peptides.

q: A 70-year-old man has had a tumor blocking his common bile duct for two months. He is jaundiced and now bleeds for a long time from a small cut. His liver cells are still healthy. What links the blocked duct to the bleeding?
options: Bilirubin in the blood destroys the circulating platelets
Without bile salts, vitamin K is poorly absorbed
The tumor releases heparin-like molecules into the blood
Blocked bile makes the liver stop making fibrinogen and albumin

why.correct: Vitamin K dissolves in fat and is absorbed only with micelles, which need bile salts. Without it, the liver still makes factors II, VII, IX and X, but in a form that cannot bind calcium and does not work. Giving vitamin K by injection bypasses the gut and corrects the bleeding.
options: Bilirubin causes the yellow color; it does not destroy platelets.
Correct. Fat malabsorption causes vitamin K deficiency.
There is no reason to think the tumor releases heparin.
Healthy hepatocytes keep making fibrinogen; the missing piece is vitamin K for the other factors.

q: Fructose enters absorptive cells by facilitated diffusion rather than with sodium. What follows from this for fructose absorption?
options: It needs the lumen to hold more fructose than the cell
Fructose absorption uses more ATP than glucose absorption
Fructose is absorbed into lacteals instead of capillaries
Fructose absorption stops when sodium is absent from the lumen

why.correct: Facilitated diffusion only moves a substance down its concentration gradient. Fructose enters while the lumen holds more than the cell, so a large dose of fructose on its own can outrun the carriers, and the unabsorbed fructose causes osmotic symptoms.
options: Correct. Without a sodium partner, fructose can only move downhill.
Facilitated diffusion uses no ATP.
Fructose leaves the cell into the villus capillaries, like glucose.
Fructose's carrier does not use sodium, so it does not depend on sodium in the lumen.

q: Some fatty acids in milk have short chains. How does their route into the body differ from that of long-chain fatty acids?
options: They cannot be absorbed at all
They are absorbed in the colon, packaged into chylomicrons
They cross the cell unchanged and enter the blood capillaries
They are absorbed in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor

why.correct: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are soluble enough in water to cross the cell without being rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged. They enter the villus capillaries and reach the liver in the hepatic portal vein, while long-chain fats go into chylomicrons and the lymph.
options: They are absorbed, and more easily than long-chain fatty acids.
They are absorbed in the small intestine, and they are not put into chylomicrons.
Correct. Their water solubility lets them take the blood route.
Intrinsic factor is for vitamin B12 only.
